new_note: *The mercy of man is toward his neighbour; but the mercy of Yahuah (God) is upon all flesh: he reproveth, and nurtureth, and teaches and brings again, as a shepherd his flock.* (Ecclesiasticus 18:13). *And when he hath found it, he layeth it on his shoulders, rejoicing.* (Luke 15:5). Sirach says the mercy of Yahuah (God) does what a shepherd does: it reproves, it nurtures, it teaches, and it brings the flock back again. Yahusha (Jesus) tells the same thing as a story — one sheep lost, the shepherd going after it until he finds it, and the sheep carried home on his shoulders with rejoicing. The bringing again is the gathering of the lost, and the mercy that gathers is wider than the mercy of man, which reaches only as far as his neighbour.
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 18:13 — *he reproveth, and nurtureth, and teaches and brings again, as a shepherd his flock.* The bringing again is the lost sheep carried home on the shepherd's shoulders (Luke 15:5).

new_note: *The mercy of man is toward his neighbour; but the mercy of Yahuah (God) is upon all flesh: he reproveth, and nurtureth, and teaches and brings again, as a shepherd his flock.* (Ecclesiasticus 18:13). *He saith to him again the second time, Simon, son of Jonas, lovest thou me? He saith unto him, Yea, Adonai (Lord); thou knowest that I love thee. He saith unto him, Feed my sheep.* (John 21:16). The shepherd Sirach describes is Yahuah (God) himself — reproving, nurturing, teaching, bringing the flock back again. On the shore Yahusha (Jesus) does exactly that to Peter: the second asking is the reproof, the answer is the nurture, and the charge to feed my sheep is the bringing again. Then he hands that same work to the man he has just restored. The one who was brought back is sent to bring back the flock.
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 18:13 — *he reproveth, and nurtureth, and teaches and brings again, as a shepherd his flock.* The Father's own shepherding, handed to the restored Peter in *Feed my sheep* (John 21:16).

new_note: *The mercy of man is toward his neighbour; but the mercy of Yahuah (God) is upon all flesh: he reproveth, and nurtureth, and teaches and brings again, as a shepherd his flock.* (Ecclesiasticus 18:13). *Yahuah (LORD) is good to all: and his tender mercies are over all his works.* (Psalm 145:9). David sang it first: Yahuah (LORD) is good to all, and his tender mercies rest over everything he has made. Sirach sets the same truth beside the mercy of a man, which reaches only his neighbour, and shows how much wider the mercy of Yahuah (God) runs — over all flesh, as a shepherd over the whole flock. The psalm and the wisdom book are saying one thing in two voices.
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 18:13 — *the mercy of Yahuah (God) is upon all flesh.* The tender mercies over all his works in Psalm 145:9, said again.

new_note: *He has mercy on them that receive discipline, and that diligently seek after his judgments.* (Ecclesiasticus 18:14). *He saith unto him the third time, Simon, son of Jonas, lovest thou me? Peter was grieved because he said unto him the third time, Lovest thou me? And he said unto him, Adonai (Lord), thou knowest all things; thou knowest that I love thee. Yahusha (Jesus) saith unto him, Feed my sheep.* (John 21:17). Sirach says mercy falls on the one who receives discipline. Peter was grieved at the third asking — three questions answering three denials — and he did not turn away from it; he received it, and the mercy landed not as condemnation but as a charge to feed the sheep. That is the pattern Sirach names: the discipline is received, the judgments of Yahuah (God) are sought, and the mercy follows.
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 18:14 — *He has mercy on them that receive discipline.* Peter, grieved at the third asking, receives the discipline and the mercy lands as *Feed my sheep* (John 21:17).

new_note: *Learn before you speak, and use physick or ever you be sick.* (Ecclesiasticus 18:19). *Wherefore, my beloved brethren, let every man be swift to hear, slow to speak, slow to wrath:* (James 1:19). Sirach puts learning before speaking the way a wise man takes his medicine before the sickness comes — the order matters. James says the same in three strokes: swift to hear, slow to speak, slow to wrath. Both put the ear ahead of the mouth, and both treat it as wisdom you practice before the moment arrives, not after.
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 18:19 — *Learn before you speak, and use physick or ever you be sick.* Learning before speaking is James' *swift to hear, slow to speak* (James 1:19).

new_note: *Let nothing hinder you to pay your vow in due time, and defer not until death to be justified.* (Ecclesiasticus 18:22). *When thou vowest a vow unto Elohim (God), defer not to pay it; for he hath no pleasure in fools: pay that which thou hast vowed.* (Ecclesiastes 5:4). Solomon wrote the rule: a vow made to Elohim (God) is to be paid without delay, because he has no pleasure in fools. Sirach is holding that rule when he tells his son to let nothing hinder the paying of a vow in due time, and he presses it one step further — do not put off until death the matter of being justified before Yahuah (God). The vow deferred and the turning deferred are the same folly.
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 18:22 — *Let nothing hinder you to pay your vow in due time.* The rule of Ecclesiastes 5:4, *defer not to pay it*, carried into Sirach's counsel.

new_note: *Go not after your lusts, but refrain thyself from your appetites.* (Ecclesiasticus 18:30). *This I say then, Walk in the Spirit, and ye shall not fulfil the lust of the flesh.* (Galatians 5:16). Sirach tells his son to refrain himself from his appetites rather than follow his lusts. Paul tells the Galatians how that refraining is done: walk in the Spirit, and the lust of the flesh will not be fulfilled. The Spirit does not loosen the standard Sirach set; he supplies the strength to keep it. Walking in the Spirit is the way a man refrains himself, and the commandments are where that walk goes.
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 18:30 — *Go not after your lusts, but refrain thyself from your appetites.* The refraining Sirach commands is done by walking in the Spirit (Galatians 5:16).

new_note: *Admonish a friend, it may be he has not done it: and if he have done it, that he do it no more.* (Ecclesiasticus 19:13). *Moreover if thy brother shall trespass against thee, go and tell him his fault between thee and him alone: if he shall hear thee, thou hast gained thy brother.* (Matthew 18:15). Sirach's counsel is to go to the friend first, because he may not have done it at all, and if he has, so that he will do it no more. Yahusha (Jesus) makes that the first step when a brother trespasses: go to him alone, tell him his fault, and if he hears you the brother is gained. Both aim at restoration, not at shame or gossip — the private word comes before anything else, and the Torah had already told a man to rebuke his neighbour rather than carry a grudge against him in his heart.
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 19:13 — *Admonish a friend, it may be he has not done it.* The private first step of Matthew 18:15 — go to him alone, and he may be gained.

new_note: *Admonish a friend: for many times it is a slander, and believe not every tale.* (Ecclesiasticus 19:15). *But if he will not hear thee, then take with thee one or two more, that in the mouth of two or three witnesses every word may be established.* (Matthew 18:16). Sirach warns that many a report is slander and that not every tale should be believed — so go and admonish the friend rather than take the story as settled. Yahusha (Jesus) builds the same safeguard into the second step: if the brother will not hear, bring one or two more, so that every word is established in the mouth of two or three witnesses. The witnesses protect the accused from a false charge and the accuser from his own inflated one. What Sirach counseled as wisdom, the King set as procedure, and both rest on the Torah's rule that one witness is never enough.
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 19:15 — *for many times it is a slander, and believe not every tale.* The two or three witnesses of Matthew 18:16 guard against the slander Sirach warns of.

new_note: *Admonish your neighbour before you threaten him; and not being angry, give place to the law of the Most High.* (Ecclesiasticus 19:17). *Moreover if thy brother shall trespass against thee, go and tell him his fault between thee and him alone: if he shall hear thee, thou hast gained thy brother.* (Matthew 18:15). Sirach sets the order and the temper together: admonish before you threaten, and do it without anger, letting the law of the Most High govern the matter rather than your own heat. That is the spirit of the first step Yahusha (Jesus) gives — go to the brother alone and tell him his fault, which is admonition, not threat. The goal is to gain the brother, and a man cannot gain his brother while he is angry at him. The rebuke works when the Torah, not the rebuker's temper, is what it stands on.
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 19:17 — *Admonish your neighbour before you threaten him.* The order and the temper of the private word in Matthew 18:15 — admonish first, and not in anger.

new_note: *A man may be known by his look, and one that has understanding by his countenance, when you meetest him.* (Ecclesiasticus 19:29). *Ye shall know them by their fruits. Do men gather grapes of thorns, or figs of thistles?* (Matthew 7:16). Sirach says a man can be known by his look, and a man of understanding by his countenance, before he has said a word. Yahusha (Jesus) gives the surer test: you will know them by their fruits, because thorns do not yield grapes. Both say the same thing about the inward man — what is in him comes out where it can be seen, whether in the face or in the fruit.
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 19:29 — *A man may be known by his look.* What is inward shows outwardly; *Ye shall know them by their fruits* (Matthew 7:16).

new_note: *It is much better to reprove, than to be angry secretly: and he that confesseth his fault shall be preserved from hurt.* (Ecclesiasticus 20:2). *And if he shall neglect to hear them, tell it unto the church: but if he neglect to hear the church, let him be unto thee as an heathen man and a publican.* (Matthew 18:17). Sirach says open reproof is far better than secret anger, and the man who confesses his fault when reproved is preserved from hurt. That is what the third step in Matthew is for: when the private word and the witnesses have both been refused, the matter is told to the assembly in the open, where it can still be confessed and the brother still preserved. Secret anger restores no one. Open reproof, met with confession, does — and only when even the assembly is refused does the brother put himself outside.
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 20:2 — *It is much better to reprove, than to be angry secretly.* The open reproof before the assembly in Matthew 18:17 — the alternative to secret anger that restores no one.

new_note: *There is one that keepeth silence, and is found wise: and another by much babbling becometh hateful.* (Ecclesiasticus 20:5). *Even a fool, when he holdeth his peace, is counted wise: and he that shutteth his lips is esteemed a man of understanding.* (Proverbs 17:28). Solomon noticed that even a fool who holds his peace is counted wise. Sirach says it from the other side: one man keeps silence and is found wise, another babbles and makes himself hateful. Both are telling the same thing — the mouth gives a man away, and the one who can shut it is already halfway to understanding.
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 20:5 — *There is one that keepeth silence, and is found wise.* The same paradox as Proverbs 17:28 — the fool who holds his peace is counted wise.

new_note: *Wisdom that is hid, and treasure that is hoarded up, what profit is in them both?* (Ecclesiasticus 20:30). *Again, the kingdom of heaven is like unto treasure hid in a field; the which when a man hath found, he hideth, and for joy thereof goeth and selleth all that he hath, and buyeth that field.* (Matthew 13:44). Sirach asks what good hidden wisdom or hoarded treasure does anyone — none, until it is found and brought out. Yahusha (Jesus) tells of treasure hidden in a field, and of the man who finds it and sells everything he has to buy the field, because treasure found is worth all of it. The man who buys the field is the one who paid the whole price: the Father, through the Son, finding his own scattered through the field of the world and giving everything to obtain them. The point Sirach made holds either way — hidden treasure profits no one until someone finds it, and finding it is worth everything.
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 20:30 — *Wisdom that is hid, and treasure that is hoarded up, what profit is in them both.* The treasure hid in the field is found and bought with everything (Matthew 13:44).
flag: Kept the old note's reading of the man who buys the field as the Father through the Son paying the whole price for the scattered seed hidden in the field of the world; stated plainly, not as settled. Author may want to check it.

new_note: *My son, have you sinned? do so no more, but ask pardon for your former sins.* (Ecclesiasticus 21:1). *For John came unto you in the way of righteousness, and ye believed him not: but the publicans and the harlots believed him: and ye, when ye had seen it, repented not afterward, that ye might believe him.* (Matthew 21:32). Sirach opens the chapter with the whole of repentance in one line: stop doing it, and ask pardon for what is past. That is what John came preaching in the wilderness, and Yahusha (Jesus) names who actually did it — the publicans and the harlots believed him and turned, while the chief priests and elders saw it and repented not. The ones with the least standing walked Sirach's counsel; the ones holding the office refused it. Sonship is shown by the turning, not by the title.
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 21:1 — *have you sinned? do so no more, but ask pardon for your former sins.* The repentance John preached — the publicans and harlots did it, the office refused it (Matthew 21:32).
flag: Old note quoted part of 21:2 (Flee from sin as from the face of a serpent) as if it were 21:1; the card's point sits in 21:1 alone, so only 21:1 is quoted.

new_note: *My son, have you sinned? do so no more, but ask pardon for your former sins.* (Ecclesiasticus 21:1). *Forsake the foolish, and live; and go in the way of understanding.* (Proverbs 9:6). Wisdom's call in Proverbs is to forsake the foolish and live, and to walk in the way of understanding. Sirach opens his chapter with the same turn, put as a father puts it to a son — if you have sinned, do so no more, and ask pardon. Forsaking and turning are one motion; the way of understanding begins where the former sins are left behind.
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 21:1 — *do so no more, but ask pardon for your former sins.* The turn Wisdom calls for in Proverbs 9:6 — forsake the foolish, and live.

new_note: *He that keepeth the law of Yahuah (God) getteth the understanding thereof: and the perfection of the fear of Yahuah (God) is wisdom.* (Ecclesiasticus 21:11). *The fear of Yahuah (LORD) is the beginning of wisdom: and the knowledge of the holy is understanding.* (Proverbs 9:10). Solomon set the foundation: the fear of Yahuah (LORD) is the beginning of wisdom. Sirach shows where it goes — the one who keeps the law of Yahuah (God) gets understanding of it, and the fear of Yahuah (God) brought to its perfection is wisdom itself. Fear is the beginning, keeping the law is the road, and wisdom is the crown of it. Understanding comes to the one who keeps, not to the one who only studies.
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 21:11 — *He that keepeth the law of Yahuah (God) getteth the understanding thereof.* The fear of Yahuah (LORD) that begins wisdom in Proverbs 9:10 is made perfect in keeping the law.

new_note: *The inner parts of a fool are like a broken vessel, and he will hold no knowledge as long as he lives.* (Ecclesiasticus 21:14). *Woe unto you, lawyers! for ye have taken away the key of knowledge: ye entered not in yourselves, and them that were entering in ye hindered.* (Luke 11:52). Sirach pictures the fool's inward parts as a broken vessel: pour knowledge in and it runs out, so he holds none his whole life. Yahusha (Jesus) says the lawyers had taken away the key of knowledge — they had not entered themselves and were hindering those who were entering. A man who holds no knowledge cannot open the door for anyone else. The key that was taken away is the Torah read plainly, and the fences the office built around it are what kept the people outside; the woe is on the office that did it, not on the people it shut out.
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 21:14 — *The inner parts of a fool are like a broken vessel.* The lawyers who took away the key of knowledge held none themselves (Luke 11:52).

new_note: *If a skilful man hear a wise word, he will commend it, and add to it: but as soon as one of no understanding heareth it, it displeaseth him, and he casteth it behind his back.* (Ecclesiasticus 21:15). *Woe unto you, lawyers! for ye have taken away the key of knowledge: ye entered not in yourselves, and them that were entering in ye hindered.* (Luke 11:52). Sirach describes two hearers: the skilful man hears a wise word and commends it and adds to it, while the man of no understanding is displeased by it and throws it behind his back. The lawyers in Luke are the second man — they heard the Word, refused it, and then took the key away so that those entering were hindered too. Casting the word behind your back is bad enough; shutting the door from the outside against others is what draws the woe. The system that does this is what Yahusha (Jesus) names; the people kept from the door are the ones he came for.
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 21:15 — *it displeaseth him, and he casteth it behind his back.* The word cast behind the back, then the key of knowledge taken away from those entering (Luke 11:52).

new_note: *A slothful man is compared to a filthy stone, and every one will hiss him out to his disgrace.* (Ecclesiasticus 22:1). *His lord answered and said unto him, Thou wicked and slothful servant, thou knewest that I reap where I sowed not, and gather where I have not strawed:* (Matthew 25:26). Sirach's picture is blunt: a slothful man is a filthy stone, and everyone hisses him out to his disgrace. The lord in the parable is just as blunt with the servant who buried his talent — wicked and slothful, he calls him, because the servant knew what his master expected and did nothing. The fault in both is the same: not wickedness done, but the work left undone. Sloth is treated as disgrace in the wisdom book and as judgment in the parable, and it is the same sin in both.
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 22:1 — *A slothful man is compared to a filthy stone.* The *wicked and slothful servant* of Matthew 25:26 — the work left undone is the disgrace.

new_note: *Whoso teaches a fool is as one that glueth a potsherd together, and as he that waketh one from a sound sleep.* (Ecclesiasticus 22:7). *Give not that which is holy unto the dogs, neither cast ye your pearls before swine, lest they trample them under their feet, and turn again and rend you.* (Matthew 7:6). Sirach says teaching a fool is like gluing a broken pot back together, or waking a man out of a dead sleep — the effort does not hold. Yahusha (Jesus) says it as a command: do not give what is holy to dogs or cast pearls before swine, because they will trample them and turn and rend you. Both know that some hearers cannot receive, and that the holy thing is wasted and the teacher is harmed when it is pressed on them. The proclamation goes out broadly, but the pursuit ends where the rejection lands.
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 22:7 — *Whoso teaches a fool is as one that glueth a potsherd together.* The futility of teaching the one who cannot receive; *neither cast ye your pearls before swine* (Matthew 7:6).

new_note: *He that telleth a tale to a fool speaks to one in a slumber: when he has told his tale, he will say, What is the matter?* (Ecclesiasticus 22:8). *Give not that which is holy unto the dogs, neither cast ye your pearls before swine, lest they trample them under their feet, and turn again and rend you.* (Matthew 7:6). Sirach says telling a tale to a fool is talking to a man asleep — when you have finished he asks what you were saying. Yahusha (Jesus) sharpens that into a command about the holy things: do not cast pearls before swine, who will trample them and turn on you. The wisdom book had been teaching discernment of the hearer for centuries; the gospel makes it a rule for the citizens of the kingdom. We speak the truth wherever the Father sends us, and when it is refused we shake the dust off and go on.
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 22:8 — *He that telleth a tale to a fool speaks to one in a slumber.* Discernment of the hearer, made a kingdom rule in Matthew 7:6.

new_note: *As timber girt and bound together in a building cannot be loosed with shaking: so the heart that is stablished by advised counsel shall fear at no time.* (Ecclesiasticus 22:16). *Therefore whosoever heareth these sayings of mine, and doeth them, I will liken him unto a wise man, which built his house upon a rock:* (Matthew 7:24). Sirach says a heart established by sound counsel is like timber girded and bound into a building — shake it and it does not come loose, so it fears nothing. Yahusha (Jesus) says the wise man is the one who hears his sayings and does them, and he likens him to a house built on a rock. The counsel that establishes the heart is the King's sayings, and the doing of them is what binds the timber. Hearing alone leaves the building loose.
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 22:16 — *so the heart that is stablished by advised counsel shall fear at no time.* The hearer and doer who built on the rock (Matthew 7:24) has the heart Sirach describes.

new_note: *As timber girt and bound together in a building cannot be loosed with shaking: so the heart that is stablished by advised counsel shall fear at no time.* (Ecclesiasticus 22:16). *He is like a man which built an house, and digged deep, and laid the foundation on a rock: and when the flood arose, the stream beat vehemently upon that house, and could not shake it: for it was founded upon a rock.* (Luke 6:48). Sirach's picture is timber bound together in a building that cannot be loosed with shaking; the heart established by counsel is like that. Luke adds a detail Matthew does not: the wise builder dug deep and laid his foundation on a rock, and when the flood beat on the house it could not shake it. The digging deep is the doing — the hearer who does the sayings is driving his foundation down to rock. That is how a heart is established so that it fears at no time.
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 22:16 — *As timber girt and bound together in a building cannot be loosed with shaking.* Luke 6:48's builder *digged deep*, and the stream *could not shake* the house.

new_note: *A heart settled upon a thought of understanding is as a fair plaistering on the wall of a gallery.* (Ecclesiasticus 22:17). *Therefore whosoever heareth these sayings of mine, and doeth them, I will liken him unto a wise man, which built his house upon a rock:* (Matthew 7:24). Sirach says a heart settled on a thought of understanding is like fine plaster on the wall of a gallery — finished, smooth, holding. Yahusha (Jesus) says the wise man is the one who hears his sayings and does them, and likens him to a house built on rock. The settled heart and the house on rock are the same man: his heart has come to rest on the King's words, and the building he is stands.
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 22:17 — *A heart settled upon a thought of understanding.* The settled heart is the hearer and doer of Matthew 7:24.

new_note: *Pales set on an high place will never stand against the wind: so a fearful heart in the imagination of a fool cannot stand against any fear.* (Ecclesiasticus 22:18). *And the rain descended, and the floods came, and the winds blew, and beat upon that house; and it fell not: for it was founded upon a rock.* (Matthew 7:25). Sirach gives the opposite picture: pales set on a height will never stand against the wind, and the fearful heart of a fool cannot stand against any fear. Matthew says the rain came down, the floods came, the winds blew and beat on the house, and it did not fall because it stood on rock. The same wind that cannot move the house on the rock blows the pales flat. The difference is not the wind but the foundation, and the foundation is hearing and doing.
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 22:18 — *so a fearful heart in the imagination of a fool cannot stand against any fear.* The wind of Matthew 7:25 that cannot move the house on the rock blows the pales flat.

new_note: *Pales set on an high place will never stand against the wind: so a fearful heart in the imagination of a fool cannot stand against any fear.* (Ecclesiasticus 22:18). *But he that heareth, and doeth not, is like a man that without a foundation built an house upon the earth; against which the stream did beat vehemently, and immediately it fell; and the ruin of that house was great.* (Luke 6:49). Sirach says pales set on a high place never stand against the wind, and the fool's fearful heart stands against nothing. Luke names the fool: he heard and did not do, and built his house on the earth with no foundation, and when the stream beat on it the house fell at once and the ruin was great. Hearing without doing is the house without a foundation. The wind finds it, and there is nothing underneath to hold.
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 22:18 — *Pales set on an high place will never stand against the wind.* The hearer who does not do, *without a foundation*, falls and the ruin is great (Luke 6:49).

new_note: *Accustom not your mouth to swearing; neither use thyself to the naming of the Holy One.* (Ecclesiasticus 23:9). *Again, ye have heard that it hath been said by them of old time, Thou shalt not forswear thyself, but shalt perform unto Yahuah (Lord) thine oaths:* (Matthew 5:33). Sirach tells his son not to let his mouth grow used to swearing, nor to make a habit of naming the Holy One. Yahusha (Jesus) begins from what they had heard said of old — do not forswear yourself, perform your oaths to Yahuah (Lord) — and goes on to say swear not at all, let your yes be yes and your no be no. He is not loosening the Torah on oaths; he is cutting away the habit Sirach warned of, the casual oath that made the name common and the word cheap. Speech that is true needs no oath to prop it up.
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 23:9 — *Accustom not your mouth to swearing.* The casual oath Sirach warns against is what Matthew 5:33 begins to cut away.

new_note: *Accustom not your mouth to swearing; neither use thyself to the naming of the Holy One.* (Ecclesiasticus 23:9). *Woe unto you, ye blind guides, which say, Whosoever shall swear by the temple, it is nothing; but whosoever shall swear by the gold of the temple, he is a debtor!* (Matthew 23:16). Sirach's counsel is simple: do not get your mouth used to swearing or to naming the Holy One. The tradition Yahusha (Jesus) is answering had gone the other way — it had built grades of oath, where swearing by the temple meant nothing but swearing by the gold of the temple bound you. The Torah knows no such grades; every vow binds and every oath counts. Sirach stood with the Torah on this, and the blind guides are the office that built the ladder of evasions, not the people who were taught to climb it.
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 23:9 — *neither use thyself to the naming of the Holy One.* Every oath counts; the graded oaths of Matthew 23:16 are the evasion Sirach's counsel never allowed.

new_note: *For as a servant that is continually beaten shall not be without a blue mark: so he that sweareth and nameth Yahuah (God) continually shall not be faultless.* (Ecclesiasticus 23:10). *But I say unto you, Swear not at all; neither by heaven; for it is Elohim's (God’s) throne:* (Matthew 5:34). Sirach says a servant who is beaten every day is never without a bruise, and a man who swears and names Yahuah (God) continually is never clean of fault — the habit leaves its mark. Yahusha (Jesus) says swear not at all, not even by heaven, because heaven is the throne of Elohim (God). To swear by heaven lightly is to drag the throne into common talk. The mark Sirach describes is what casual swearing does to a man, and the command in Matthew is how it stops.
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 23:10 — *he that sweareth and nameth Yahuah (God) continually shall not be faultless.* The mark habitual swearing leaves; *Swear not at all; neither by heaven* (Matthew 5:34).

new_note: *A man that useth much swearing shall be filled with iniquity, and the plague shall never depart from his house: if he shall offend, his sin shall be upon him: and if he acknowledge not his sin, he makes a double offence: and if he swear in vain, he shall not be innocent, but his house shall be full of calamities.* (Ecclesiasticus 23:11). *But let your communication be, Yea, yea; Nay, nay: for whatsoever is more than these cometh of evil.* (Matthew 5:37). Sirach traces what much swearing does to a man: he is filled with iniquity, the plague does not leave his house, and every oath sworn in vain adds to the account. Yahusha (Jesus) names the root in one line — whatever is more than yes and no comes of evil. The iniquity Sirach saw filling the swearer's house and the evil Yahusha (Jesus) names at the source are the same thing seen from two ends. Plain speech, yes and no, is the way out of both.
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 23:11 — *A man that useth much swearing shall be filled with iniquity.* The iniquity that fills the swearer is the evil Matthew 5:37 names at the root.

new_note: *A man that useth much swearing shall be filled with iniquity, and the plague shall never depart from his house: if he shall offend, his sin shall be upon him: and if he acknowledge not his sin, he makes a double offence: and if he swear in vain, he shall not be innocent, but his house shall be full of calamities.* (Ecclesiasticus 23:11). *And he that shall swear by heaven, sweareth by the throne of Elohim (God), and by him that sitteth thereon.* (Matthew 23:22). Sirach says the man who swears much is filled with iniquity and his house is full of calamities — he takes every oath seriously, because every one of them counts. Yahusha (Jesus) says the same against the tradition that had sorted oaths into binding and empty: to swear by heaven is to swear by the throne of Elohim (God) and by him who sits on it, so there is no empty oath. Sirach and Yahusha (Jesus) stand together on the Torah here; the grading of oaths was the invention of the system, not of Moses.
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 23:11 — *and if he swear in vain, he shall not be innocent.* No oath is empty — to swear by heaven is to swear by the throne (Matthew 23:22).

new_note: *Such a man only fears the eyes of men, and knoweth not that the eyes of Yahuah (God) are ten thousand times brighter than the sun, beholding all the ways of men, and considering the most secret parts.* (Ecclesiasticus 23:19). *For the ear of jealousy heareth all things: and the noise of murmurings is not hid.* (Wisdom of Solomon 1:10). Sirach describes the man who fears only the eyes of men and forgets that the eyes of Yahuah (God) are ten thousand times brighter than the sun, searching out the most secret places. The Wisdom of Solomon says the same of his hearing — the ear of jealousy hears everything, and murmuring is not hidden. Nothing done in the dark and nothing muttered under the breath escapes him. The two books together close every hiding place: he sees what the walls cover and hears what the voice keeps low.
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 23:19 — *the eyes of Yahuah (God) are ten thousand times brighter than the sun.* The eyes that see the secret parts and the ear that hears all murmuring (Wisdom of Solomon 1:10).

new_note: *Her children shall not take root, and her branches shall bring forth no fruit.* (Ecclesiasticus 23:25). *And when he saw a fig tree in the way, he came to it, and found nothing thereon, but leaves only, and said unto it, Let no fruit grow on thee henceforward for ever. And presently the fig tree withered away.* (Matthew 21:19). Sirach says of the adulterous woman that her children will not take root and her branches will bring forth no fruit — what grows from unfaithfulness has nothing underneath it, and nothing comes of it. Yahusha (Jesus) came to the fig tree, found leaves and no fruit, and spoke the same sentence over it: let no fruit grow on you from now on. The tree stands for the leadership that held the vineyard in trust and gave the Father leaves instead of fruit, as the parable of the husbandmen later in the same chapter says plainly. No root, no fruit, and then no fruit forever — the judgment reads the same in both books.
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 23:25 — *Her children shall not take root, and her branches shall bring forth no fruit.* Leaves without fruit; the fig tree told *Let no fruit grow on thee henceforward for ever* (Matthew 21:19).
flag: Sirach 23:25 is spoken of the adulterous woman's children; the tie to the cursed fig tree is the shared sentence of no root and no fruit on unfaithfulness. Kept as the old note had it, said plainly.

new_note: *I came out of the mouth of the Most High, and covered the earth as a cloud.* (Ecclesiasticus 24:3). *But straightway Yahusha (Jesus) spake unto them, saying, Be of good cheer; it is I; be not afraid.* (Matthew 14:27). Wisdom says she came out of the mouth of the Most High and covered the earth as a cloud. The one who came out of the Father's mouth is the Word the Father spoke — the Formed one beside the formless Maker — and the prophets knew him as the one who rides the clouds. On the water Yahusha (Jesus) says to the frightened men, it is I, the same words he uses when he says that before Abraham was, I am. The Wisdom that came out of the mouth of the Most High is the one walking on the sea, and he tells them not to be afraid.
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 24:3 — *I came out of the mouth of the Most High, and covered the earth as a cloud.* The Word from the Father's mouth is the one on the water saying *it is I* (Matthew 14:27).
flag: Kept the old note's reading of Matthew 14:27's *it is I* as the Formed Wisdom of Ecclesiasticus 24 naming himself, with John 8:58 alongside. Live text reads *Most High* where the old note had *most High*.

new_note: *So the Creator of all things gave me a commandment, and he that made me caused my tabernacle to rest, and said, Let your dwelling be in Jacob, and your inheritance in Yashar'el (Israel).* (Ecclesiasticus 24:8). *For the kingdom of heaven is like unto a man that is an householder, which went out early in the morning to hire labourers into his vineyard.* (Matthew 20:1). Wisdom was commanded by the Creator to pitch her tent in Jacob and take her inheritance in Yashar'el (Israel). Isaiah had already said that the vineyard of Yahuah (God) is the house of Yashar'el (Israel), and Jeremiah mourned the pastors who destroyed it. When Yahusha (Jesus) opens the parable with a householder hiring labourers into his vineyard, that is the vineyard he means — the covenant people the Father planted and in whom Wisdom made her dwelling. The householder is the Father, and the labourers are the ones he calls into it through the hours of the day.
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 24:8 — *Let your dwelling be in Jacob, and your inheritance in Yashar'el (Israel).* Wisdom planted in Yashar'el (Israel), the vineyard the householder hires labourers into (Matthew 20:1).

new_note: *He created me from the beginning before the world, and I shall never fail.* (Ecclesiasticus 24:9). *For by him were all things created, that are in heaven, and that are in earth, visible and invisible, whether they be thrones, or dominions, or principalities, or powers: all things were created by him, and for him:* (Colossians 1:16). Wisdom says she was brought forth from the beginning, before the world, and that she will never fail. Paul says of the Son that all things in heaven and earth were created by him and for him — he is before all things, and everything holds together in him. These are one and the same: the Wisdom beside the Maker before the world is the Formed one through whom the all things were made, the Son who has a Father and is before every creature. Not a second co-equal Elohim (God) beside the Father, but the Word the Father brought forth, who came in flesh as Yahusha (Jesus).
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 24:9 — *He created me from the beginning before the world, and I shall never fail.* Wisdom before the world is the Son by whom all things were created (Colossians 1:16).

new_note: *And I took root in an honourable people, even in the portion of the inheritance of Yahuah (God).* (Ecclesiasticus 24:12). *For the kingdom of heaven is like unto a man that is an householder, which went out early in the morning to hire labourers into his vineyard.* (Matthew 20:1). Wisdom says she took root in an honourable people, in the portion that is Yahuah's (God's) own inheritance. That people is the vineyard of the parable — the householder's own ground, into which he goes out to hire labourers through the day. The vineyard is Yashar'el (Israel), and so are the labourers called into it, whether called early or late: the covenant line from Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, and the children of that line who grew up scattered among the nations and are being called home. The honourable people Wisdom rooted in is the inheritance the Father is still gathering.
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 24:12 — *I took root in an honourable people.* The honourable people is the vineyard of Matthew 20:1 — Yashar'el (Israel), the Father's own inheritance.

new_note: *As the vine brought I forth pleasant savour, and my flowers are the fruit of honour and riches.* (Ecclesiasticus 24:17). *I am the true vine, and my Father is the husbandman.* (John 15:1). In the great hymn of Wisdom she calls herself a vine, bringing forth pleasant savour, her flowers the fruit of honour and riches — the same Wisdom the Creator commanded to take root in Jacob, and whom Sirach goes on to name as the book of the covenant, the law Moses commanded. Yahusha (Jesus) says I am the true vine, and my Father is the husbandman. The Wisdom planted as a vine in Yashar'el (Israel) is the one who stood on the earth and said so; the Word that became flesh is the vine the branches abide in and bear from. The husbandman is the Father, and the vine is his Formed one.
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 24:17 — *As the vine brought I forth pleasant savour.* The vine of Wisdom planted in Jacob is the true vine of John 15:1.

new_note: *Come to me, all you that be desirous of me, and fill yourselves with my fruits.* (Ecclesiasticus 24:19). *The Son of Adam came eating and drinking, and they say, Behold a man gluttonous, and a winebibber, a friend of publicans and sinners. But wisdom is justified of her children.* (Matthew 11:19). Wisdom calls out: come to me, all you who desire me, and fill yourselves with my fruits. Yahusha (Jesus) came eating and drinking, and the ones who came to him were the publicans and the sinners, while the system called him a glutton and a winebibber — and then he says wisdom is justified of her children. The children of wisdom are the ones who heard the call and came to be filled. The invitation Sirach wrote down is the one the Son of Adam spoke in Galilee, and his table was where the filling happened.
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 24:19 — *Come to me, all you that be desirous of me.* Wisdom's invitation; *wisdom is justified of her children* who came (Matthew 11:19).
